meta.title: Who really said “We Don't Know Who Discovered Water, But We Know It Wasn't a Fish”? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Einstein and not McLuhan. The line was printed in 1966 as a remark by Father John Culkin — and Einstein's real fish sentence is a different one.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We Don't Know Who Discovered Water, But We Know It Wasn't a Fish'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Einstein, not McLuhan. Printed in 1966 as a remark by Father John Culkin. Einstein's real fish sentence, from 1936, is different.

answer.label: Not Einstein — first credited in print to Father John Culkin
answer.authorDates: 1928–1993 · American media scholar; a Jesuit priest at Fordham when the line was printed
answer.sourceLine: The earliest appearance of this exact wording that anyone has dated is April 1966, in Ramparts magazine, where Howard Gossage quotes it as a saying of “Father John Culkin of Fordham, a leading McLuhanite”. Marshall McLuhan — the other name it gets pinned on — used the line himself later that year and in 1967, but each time he credited it to someone else: “someone said once”, “a wit has said”. Einstein is nowhere in the chain. Quote Investigator ↗ lays the whole sequence out, and it starts with a proverb about fish that was already in print in 1909.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — not Einstein’s, and even Culkin’s claim is a credit given by others, not one he made.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Howard Gossage, “Understanding Marshall McLuhan”, April 1966 — quoting Father John Culkin
“It is said that fish do not see water, nor do Polar bears feel the cold” — Every-Day Japan (1909), introduction by Count Hayashi
“What does a fish know about the water in which he swims all his life?” — “Self-Portrait”, an essay dated 1936

source.excerpt: In the ordinary course of events, we are not aware of our environment any more than a fish is aware of his. As Father John Culkin of Fordham, a leading McLuhanite, says, “We don’t know who it was discovered water, but we’re pretty sure it wasn’t a fish.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that “Marshall McLuhan did use a version of this saying in speeches by 1966, but he credited ‘someone’ or ‘a wit’”, and that in 1966 “John Culkin was credited with a version that closely matched” the familiar one. Einstein does not appear anywhere in QI’s chain of attribution.

The idea is older than the sentence and is catalogued as a modern proverb. QI cites The Dictionary of Modern Proverbs supplement for “A fish doesn’t know it is in water”, whose first citation is Every-Day Japan (1909) ↗: “It is said that fish do not see water, nor do Polar bears feel the cold.” A 1915 novel, The Cheerful Blackguard ↗, inverts it into “an inventive fish, who discovered water”.

John M. Culkin ↗ was a real and well-placed candidate: a Jesuit at Fordham who had met McLuhan at Harvard, brought him to Fordham for a year in 1964, and later founded the Center for Understanding Media. The credit to him is repeated in The Medium is the Massage (1967) by McLuhan and Quentin Fiore, and again in Edmund Carpenter’s They Became What They Beheld (1970).

Einstein’s own fish line is real, and it is not this one. In the short essay “Self-Portrait”, dated 1936 and collected in Out of My Later Years, he wrote: “Of what is significant in one’s own existence one is hardly aware … What does a fish know about the water in which he swims all his life?” Same thought, different sentence, and no punchline about who discovered it.
source.excerptNote: Note what this is: Gossage reporting something Culkin said, in a magazine article about McLuhan. It is a credit given by a third party, not a claim Culkin made in print himself — which is why the attribution has never fully settled. Writing in The Atlantic in 1974, Warren Hinkle observed that Culkin “may even have said that, but primary authorship was as difficult to trace in quotations favored by Gossage as the authorship of the Dead Sea Scrolls”.

source.rightsNote: The proverb this descends from is long out of copyright — the 1909 and 1915 printings are both public domain in the United States. The specific sentence on this page is not one of those: its earliest known publication is 1966, well after the 1931 cut-off, so we treat it as in copyright and name the person it was credited to rather than claiming a status we cannot support.

author.name: John M. Culkin
author.heading: About John M. Culkin
author.metaLine: 1928–1993 · American media scholar, educator and Jesuit priest
author.bio: Culkin was a Brooklyn-born Jesuit who took a doctorate in education at Harvard, met Marshall McLuhan there, and in 1964 persuaded Fordham to bring him to New York for a year — which is how the two men were in the same room when this line started circulating. He left the priesthood in 1969 and founded the Center for Understanding Media, and is often described as the person who invented media literacy as a school subject. He is remembered rather less for the aphorism his friends kept quoting in his name.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This one has collected three separate false or shaky credits, and the most famous name has the weakest claim of the three.

items.why: Nothing in QI’s chain of citations ↗ connects Einstein to this saying at any date. The credit appears to be pure gravitational pull: the sentence sounds like an aphorism about perception, so it drifted to the most quotable scientist available.

McLuhan used the line at a symposium in November 1966 and in a Toronto speech in March 1967 — and on both occasions attributed it to somebody else (“Someone said once…”, “A wit has said…”). A speaker at that same 1966 symposium promptly credited it back to McLuhan the following day, which is roughly how the error was born.

Einstein did write about a fish and its water, in the 1936 essay “Self-Portrait”: “What does a fish know about the water in which he swims all his life?” It was published in English in 1950 in Out of My Later Years and quoted in the New York Times review that May. If you want an Einstein line on this theme, that is the one.

The Harvard anthropologist Clyde Kluckhohn wrote “It would hardly be fish who discovered the existence of water” in Mirror for Man (1949), and the lawyer Pierce Butler told a US Senate subcommittee in 1954 that “It wasn’t fish who discovered water.” Neither is the quoted sentence, but both predate every version that names a modern author.

misattribution.truthLine: The saying is a twentieth-century proverb with a documented first printing and a plausible named speaker — and Einstein is not that speaker at any point in the record QI assembled ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line earns its keep because it makes an abstract idea physical in nine words: the medium you are suspended in is the one thing you cannot see. That is why it attached itself to McLuhan — his whole argument was that people notice content and never notice the technology carrying it — and why it has since been borrowed by anthropology, advertising, management writing and anyone explaining unconscious bias.

Its attribution history is a decent illustration of its own point. The sentence circulated for years inside a small circle around McLuhan, credited casually and inconsistently in print, until the loudest name in the room absorbed it. Then the internet handed it to a still louder one.
detailsBody: The 1966 Ramparts article was written by Howard Gossage, a San Francisco advertising man who spent that period, in a later profile’s phrase, “schlepping McLuhan around the country” and introducing him to media executives. The fish line was one of his favourites, and he used it both crediting Culkin and, when McLuhan needed explaining, crediting McLuhan — which is exactly how a saying loses its owner.

By 1967 the credit to Culkin had been printed in The Medium is the Massage itself, McLuhan and Quentin Fiore’s book, where the line appears attributed to “John M. Culkin”. It is also on the accompanying 1968 recording — not spoken by McLuhan, QI notes, but by a voice sounding like a cartoon character.

Meanwhile the underlying proverb kept producing its own variants independently. A psychology textbook in 1960 used “The fish will be the last to discover water” and credited it to “someone”. A foreword by the Modern Language Association’s executive secretary, dated March 1966, offered “No fish ever discovered water and no monolingual speaker ever understood the unique qualities of his own language.” Nobody involved seems to have thought they were quoting a specific person.
context.pull: The medium you are suspended in is the one thing you cannot see — including, apparently, where your quotations come from.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest instance of this wording located by QI is April 1966 in Ramparts, in Howard Gossage's article 'Understanding Marshall McLuhan', where it is credited to Father John Culkin of Fordham rather than to McLuhan.
Marshall McLuhan used the saying in November 1966 and March 1967 but attributed it to 'someone' and to 'a wit' rather than claiming coinage.

The Dictionary of Modern Proverbs entry 'A fish doesn't know it is in water' has as its first citation Every-Day Japan (1909), whose introduction by Count Hayashi reads 'It is said that fish do not see water, nor do Polar bears feel the cold'.
Einstein's 1936 essay 'Self-Portrait', published in English in Out of My Later Years, contains 'What does a fish know about the water in which he swims all his life?'

Clyde Kluckhohn wrote 'It would hardly be fish who discovered the existence of water' in Mirror for Man (1949), and Pierce Butler wrote 'It wasn't fish who discovered water' in 1954 US Senate testimony.
The Medium is the Massage (1967) by McLuhan and Quentin Fiore attributes the saying to John M. Culkin, as does Edmund Carpenter's They Became What They Beheld (1970).

John M. Culkin Jr. (21 June 1928 - 23 July 1993) was an American academic and former Jesuit priest, a media scholar who came to Fordham University in 1964 and brought Marshall McLuhan there, later founding the Center for Understanding Media.
Every-Day Japan by Arthur Lloyd is available in full view at Google Books.
The Cheerful Blackguard by Roger Pocock is available in full view at Google Books.
Wikiquote's sourced Marshall McLuhan page carries his Counterblast (1969) line 'We live invested in an electric information environment that is quite as imperceptible to us as water is to fish'.
